claims.feature: other: didactic register suppresses the device
claims.claim: Gordon says that in Operation ARES the didactic purpose is so clear that ambiguity and an invitation to interpret have no place.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: an invitation to interpret have no place

claims.claim: Gordon gives the length of the four volumes of The Book of the New Sun as 1222 pages in the first editions.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)

claims.claim: Attebery says Wolfe generally invents by reusing what is forgotten rather than by coining.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy (Indiana University Press, 1992), ch. 7 'Science Fantasy'

claims.claim: Andre-Driussi says it took him eight years to sell all 1,000 copies of the first edition of Lexicon Urthus.
claims.source: Michael Andre-Driussi, interview in Ultan's Library, 2008
claims.quote: it took me eight years to sell all 1,000 copies!

claims.claim: Joan Gordon divides Wolfe criticism into macro and micro kinds and places her own work on the macro side.
claims.quote: There are two kinds of Wolfeian criticism: macro and micro

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe adjusts his style to suit an adolescent audience in The Devil in a Forest.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: Wolfe adjusts his style to suit an adolescent audience

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe adjusts his style for the adolescent audience without condescension.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe explains his unfamiliar words tactfully in the course of furthering plot or developing character rather than glossing them outright.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: he tactfully explains them in the course of furthering

claims.claim: Gordon says Wolfe's emphasis on the number of stresses rather than the number of syllables parallels early English poetry.
claims.source: Joan Gordon, Gene Wolfe (Starmont Reader's Guide 29, Starmont House, 1986)
claims.quote: number of stresses rather than upon number of syllables

claims.claim: Clute says the evidence for the impostor's substitution in The Fifth Head of Cerberus is extractable through an examination of the manuscript that tells the story.
claims.source: John Clute, 'Wolfe, Gene', The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (3rd edn, online; entry updated 13 July 2026, signed [JC])
claims.quote: extractable through an examination of the manuscript that tells the story
claims.page: SFE entry 'Wolfe, Gene', on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute writes that in all of Wolfe's greatest works faces are masques.
claims.source: John Clute, 'Wolfe, Gene', The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (3rd edn, online; entry updated 13 July 2026, signed [JC])
claims.page: SFE entry 'Wolfe, Gene', on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Joan Gordon says that as glorious as Wolfe's work is to read it is difficult to write about.
claims.source: Joan Gordon ('JG'), 'Wolfe Trap', review of Peter Wright's Attending Daedalus, Science Fiction Studies 32.1 (#95, March 2005), pp. 212-213

claims.claim: Manlove states that his book sets out to show how the deceptive surface of exciting adventures and exotic settings in science fiction may contain complex patterns of imagery and significance.
claims.source: C.N. Manlove, Science Fiction: Ten Explorations (1986), p. 4, quoted in Sarah Pell, 'Thematic Explorations', review of C.N. Manlove's Science Fiction: Ten Explorations, Science Fiction Studies #45 (July 1988)
claims.quote: the deceptive surface of exciting adventures and exotic settings

claims.claim: Donald M. Hassler reports Baird Searles' objection that beneath Wolfe's stylistic glitter there may be no real speculative ideas.
claims.source: Donald M. Hassler, 'Throwing Down the Gauntlet', review of Joan Gordon's Gene Wolfe, Science Fiction Studies #41 (March 1987)

claims.claim: Hassler credits Wolfe with a mastery of baroque complexity of reference.
claims.source: Donald M. Hassler, 'Throwing Down the Gauntlet', review of Joan Gordon's Gene Wolfe, Science Fiction Studies #41 (March 1987)
claims.quote: mastery of baroque complexity of reference

verdicts.trueWording: ambiguity and an invitation to interpret have no place
verdicts.note: Gordon ch. III 'Operation ARES', the 14/15 spread (quote sits in the right-hand column, p. 15). Raw PDF pulled from gwern.net and text-extracted with pdftotext. Full sentence names the novel's didactic purpose as so specific that this follows; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Four volumes, 1222 pages in the first editions
verdicts.note: Gordon ch. VIII 'The Book of the New Sun', immediately after the p.77 folio, i.e. p. 78. Surrounding text is about Severian and the tetralogy, so 'four volumes of The Book of the New Sun' is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe generally invents by reusing what is forgotten
verdicts.note: Attebery, Strategies of Fantasy p. 124 (running heads confirm ch. 7 'Science Fantasy' spans 105-125; ch. 8 begins at 127). The 'rather than by coining' limb is carried by the preceding sentence about introducing the new and strange through old, archaic words.

verdicts.trueWording: it took me eight years to sell all 1,000 copies
verdicts.note: Ultan's Library interview, answer to Master Ultan's question about the reception of the original Lexicon Urthus; Andre-Driussi is the speaker, and a later answer confirms the first edition's print run of 1,000.

verdicts.trueWording: two kinds of Wolfeian criticism: macro and micro
verdicts.note: Ultan's Library, 'Micro-Wolfenomics', opening sentence of the review body. Gordon places herself: she tends toward the macro, making broad claims about themes and style, while Andre-Driussi supplies the micro.

verdicts.trueWording: Wolfe adjusts his style to suit an adolescent audience
verdicts.note: Gordon ch. VI 'The Devil in a Forest', p. 44 (the 44/45 folio closes the spread). The paragraph explicitly concerns The Devil in a Forest and its medieval vocabulary.
Gordon ch. VI, p. 44, same sentence as index 799: the style is adjusted for the adolescent audience 'as well, and he does so without condescension.'

verdicts.trueWording: he tactfully explains them in the course of furthering
verdicts.note: Gordon ch. VI, p. 44. Sentence continues 'plot or developing character', and the following sentence gives the example of 'dirk' defined against 'misericorde' through a soldier's voice - i.e. explained in narrative rather than glossed outright.

verdicts.trueWording: number of stresses rather than upon number of syllables
verdicts.note: Gordon ch. VI, p. 45: 'such emphasis upon number of stresses rather than upon number of syllables parallels early English poetry.' Both OCR passes of the page carry the phrase identically.

verdicts.trueWording: extractable through an examination of the manuscript that tells the story
verdicts.note: SFE entry 'Wolfe, Gene' (updated 13 July 2026, signed [JC]), paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus. Same sentence establishes the shapeshifting alien taking the anthropologist's identity; the paragraph later calls him 'an impostor'.

verdicts.trueWording: As in all of Wolfe's greatest works, faces are masques
verdicts.note: SFE entry 'Wolfe, Gene' ([JC]), closing sentence of the Fifth Head of Cerberus paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: as glorious as his work is to read, it's difficult
verdicts.note: SFS #95 (32.1, March 2005), review 'Wolfe Trap' of Peter Wright's Attending Daedalus, signed -JG; the reviewer identifies herself by referring to 'my Starmont Reader's Guide: Gene Wolfe (1986)', i.e. Joan Gordon. Sentence ends 'to write about'. Wayback raw capture reached directly.

verdicts.trueWording: the deceptive surface of exciting adventures and exotic settings
verdicts.note: SFS #45 (15.2, July 1988), 'Thematic Explorations', signed - Sarah Pell, Florida International University. Manlove is quoted at p. 4 as undertaking to show how this surface 'may actually contain complex patterns of imagery and significance'.

verdicts.trueWording: underneath Wolfe's stylistic glitter and mastery of baroque complexity
verdicts.note: SFS #41 (14.1, March 1987), 'Throwing Down the Gauntlet', signed - Donald M. Hassler, Kent State University. Hassler reports that Gordon notes Baird Searles' objection that beneath this 'there may be no real speculative ideas'.

verdicts.trueWording: mastery of baroque complexity of reference
verdicts.note: SFS #41, 'Throwing Down the Gauntlet'. The phrase is on the page verbatim, but only inside the reported objection: 'She notes Baird Searles' objection that underneath Wolfe's stylistic glitter and mastery of baroque complexity of reference there may be no real speculative ideas...'. Hassler nowhere credits Wolfe with it in his own voice; the whole review otherwise praises Gordon's book, not Wolfe's baroque mastery. Same sentence as index 824, which attributes it correctly.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Hassler himself credits Wolfe with it - the phrase sits inside his report of Baird Searles' objection, not in his own assertion
